page.title: Gaming Headset or Mic? Which to Buy in 2026 (Headset vs Headphones + Mic)
page.h1: Gaming headset or mic: which one to buy
page.desc: Gaming headset or a separate mic? A headset covers chat on every console, and Xbox ignores USB mics. Seven headsets and mics priced on 2026-11-17.
page.answer: Short answer. Gaming headset or mic: get a headset unless you stream. Xbox ignores any USB mic without the Designed for Xbox chip, so wired chat there means a headset in the controller's 3.5 mm jack. The EKSA E900 Pro ($46.99) does that and also runs on PS5, Switch and PC.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • The desk-mic route costs about twice as much, and you still have no headphones. The Maono PD200XS set costs $43.00 more than the E900 Pro headset: $89.99 − $46.99 = $43.00, and $89.99 ÷ $46.99 = 1.92×.
  • The cheapest mic saves almost nothing. The Maono DGM20 costs $3.00 less than the E900 Pro ($46.99 − $43.99) and plays no audio.
  • A named maker for Series X|S costs more. The HyperX Cloud III costs $23.00 more than the E900 Pro ($69.99 − $46.99). HyperX names Xbox Series X|S on its product page, but EKSA names only Xbox One.
  • The cheapest Xbox headset here. The EKSA Fenrir S costs $10.00 less than the E900 Pro ($46.99 − $36.99). It gives up the USB 7.1 mode and EKSA's PC software.
  • Keeping your own headphones on Xbox. The ModMic Uni 2+ plus Antlion's Y adapter costs $64.95 + $12.95 = $77.90. That is $7.91 more than a whole Cloud III ($77.90 − $69.99).
  • A desk mic needs to sit close. The Cloud III's boom mic is rated −42 dBV and the PD200XS's XLR output −52 dBV, a 10 dB gap: −42 − (−52) = 10, and 10^(10/20) = 3.2× less voltage per pascal. That is why dynamic desk mics are spoken into from close up. FIFINE recommends 2 to 6 inches for the AM8.
  • Headset mics are good enough for chat. In SoundGuys' listener poll on the Cloud III's recorded mic samples, 77% of 2,324 votes rated it Good or Perfect (52% + 25%).

Why a USB mic goes silent on Xbox, and what works on each console

Xbox. Maono's support page says that "the Xbox operating system deliberately does not support the generic UAC standard for audio." UAC (USB Audio Class) is the plug-and-play driver that PCs and the PS5 use for USB mics. For a USB device to work on Xbox, it "must be part of the 'Designed for Xbox' licensing program," which requires an authentication chip. Without that chip, "the Xbox sees an unauthorized device and simply ignores it." Maono notes that the console is designed for a 3.5 mm headset, mic included, plugged straight into the controller. Neither Maono, FIFINE nor any USB desk mic on this page lists Xbox.

EKSA E900 Pro on Xbox. EKSA's manual says to plug the 3.5 mm cable into the newer Xbox One controller's jack. The original Xbox One controller needs a Microsoft adapter, which is not included, and the Xbox 360 is not supported. The manual also says the 7.1 surround driver "only supports Windows," so on any console the E900 Pro works as a stereo headset. The manual doesn't name Xbox Series X|S. If you want the maker to name it, choose the HyperX Cloud III.

PS5. Sony's PS5 FAQ says "most USB and analog headsets will be supported," and that headsets on the controller's 3.5 mm jack are supported. Third-party Bluetooth headsets "will not be supported." Maono and FIFINE both list PS5 for their USB mics, so on PS5 and PC you can choose either a headset or a mic based on voice quality and desk space.

Keeping your headphones. The ModMic Uni 2+ is a clip-on 3.5 mm mic. Antlion says its Y adapter lets a ModMic work through a controller's 3.5 mm port on Xbox, PlayStation, Switch and Steam Deck. Of the mic routes on this page, it is the only one that works on Xbox.
